summary: Describes problems that DNSSEC-validating resolvers and applications can hit on networks with broken or non-compliant equipment, such as devices that mangle DNS messages. It outlines ways to detect and work around these issues. It is a Best Current Practice.

eli5.summary: Some roads have broken bridges that stop special secure mail from getting through. This explains how to notice the blocked road and find a way around it.

what is a host validator in dnssec
what happens when dnssec is blocked by a middlebox
subtitle: How a DNSSEC validator can test the network and resolvers it depends on, and work around the ones that break DNSSEC.

tldr.problem: Network components such as non-compliant resolvers, DNS proxies and middleboxes often make it hard or impossible for validating resolvers to get the DNSSEC data they need.
tldr.mechanism: A Host Validator runs a set of small tests against its resolver and network, labels the resolver by what it supports, and then uses a fallback sequence (other resolvers, TCP, different EDNS0 sizes, or iterating from the root) to avoid the roadblocks.
tldr.outcome: The RFC describes tests and mitigation techniques as a shared approach but does not specify exactly how to tie them together. It also warns that turning DNSSEC off to cope with a broken network costs security.

facts.label: Answer size that fits without TCP

today: RFC 8027 is a Best Current Practice and, according to the metadata for this unit, has not been obsoleted or updated. It remains the written approach to detecting and avoiding DNSSEC roadblocks.

sections.title: Why DNSSEC Hits Roadblocks
sections.content:
RFC 8027 describes problems seen while deploying DNSSEC that come from non-compliant infrastructure, and it proposes detection and mitigation techniques. It is a Best Current Practice (BCP 207) and uses the key words MUST, SHOULD and MAY as defined in RFC 2119.

The RFC names a Host Validator: either a validating stub resolver, such as a library linked into an application, or a validating resolver daemon on the same machine. A Validating Forwarding Resolver uses upstream resolvers when possible and should run the same tests before using one.

The background lists why validation gets blocked:

  • recursive resolvers and DNS proxies that are not fully DNSSEC compliant;
  • resolvers that are not DNSSEC aware;
  • middleboxes that block, modify or restrict outbound traffic to port 53 over UDP, TCP or both;
  • in-path components that do not allow UDP fragments.

The tests cannot fix cases where a host cannot talk directly to a resolver, for example because of DNS proxies between the user and the resolver. Results can then be inconsistent.
sections.eli5: Special sealed letters sometimes get lost or opened by clumsy mail sorters on the way. This RFC is about finding out which sorters are clumsy.

sections.title: Goals
sections.content:
The goal is to show how a Host Validator can detect what a recursive resolver can do and work around problems that would affect DNSSEC resolution. That lets the validator keep using the resolver's cache, which decreases network traffic and improves response times.

A Host Validator has two choices. It can wait until real queries show problems, or it can test proactively to build a workaround list ahead of time. Each has pros and cons that depend on the application, and the RFC does not say which to use. It only says that roadblock avoidance techniques ought to be used when needed and if possible. The same tests also let a recursive resolver check whether its own upstream connections hinder validation.
sections.eli5: The aim is to keep using the helpful shared mail room when it works, and to know when to go around it.

sections.title: Testing a Recursive Resolver
sections.content:
A resolver should run these tests when it first starts, and MAY run them again after a network change such as an address change. The tests check one feature at a time. By default queries SHOULD set the Recursion Desired flag and be sent over UDP, and they MUST NOT set the DNSSEC OK (DO) bit or use other DNSSEC features such as EDNS0. There is a comprehensive set and a fast set. If the fast one passes, the comprehensive one MAY be considered passed.

Each test has a purpose, a query and a success condition. Examples:

  • UDP and TCP answers: ask for an A record of a known existing name and expect an A record in the answer. If the UDP test fails, an implementation MAY skip the rest.
  • EDNS0: send an EDNS0 OPT record and expect an EDNS0 option with version number 0 back.
  • DO bit: set the DO bit and expect it set in the response. Some resolvers pass only because they copy unknown flags, and fail later tests.
  • AD bit: for zones signed with algorithm 5 (RSASHA1) and 8 (RSASHA256), expect the Authentic Data (AD) bit set, which shows the resolver validates.
  • RRSIG, DNSKEY and DS queries: expect signatures and key records to come back. DNSKEY answers over 1220 bytes can fail without TCP, so DNS over TCP MUST be available for DNSSEC use in general.
  • NSEC and NSEC3: expect the right proof records for names that do not exist. NSEC3 with the AD bit set shows support for algorithm 7.
  • DNAME: expect the DNAME and a covering RRSIG in the answer.
  • Permissive DNSSEC: asking for data from a broken delegation must give SERVFAIL, otherwise the resolver ignores validation failures.
  • Unknown types: ask for a recently defined type or an unknown type in the 20000-22000 range and expect it back.
sections.eli5: It is a checklist of small questions. Can you hear me by phone and by letter? Do you understand the special seal? Do you say no when a seal is faked?

sections.title: Testing the Network Path Itself
sections.content:
A Host Validator may need to query authoritative servers or known open recursive resolvers directly, so some key network features MUST work.

  • Remote UDP over port 53: a query to a distant authoritative server for a record it holds should return the A record.
  • Remote UDP with fragmentation: a query whose answer is larger than 2000 bytes, such as the DNSKEY record with the DO bit set, tests whether fragmented UDP answers arrive. A failure here is not serious if TCP works.
  • Outbound TCP over port 53: the same query over TCP should work.

A further test checks which DS and DNSKEY algorithm combinations a resolver supports, using test names of the form ds-N.alg-M-nsec.test.example.com. Success is an answer with the AD bit set and a matching record type. The notes say that NSEC is not defined for algorithms 6 and 7, so an NSEC3 name is needed there, and that NSEC3 is not defined for algorithms 1, 3 and 5.

All tests assume the path is free of DNS-interfering middleboxes and that the tested address is a unicast or an identically configured anycast address. The tests may reveal such interference but the RFC does not say how to work around it.
sections.eli5: Besides asking the mail room, you also check that the roads out of town are open for small and big parcels.

sections.title: Labeling the Results
sections.content: The test results are aggregated into broad labels for a resolver. A resolver may fall between them, so the label is extended with the word Partial before Validator or DNSSEC-aware, followed by sub-descriptors of what is not working: Unknown, DNAME, NSEC3, TCP, SlowBig (UDP is size limited but TCP fallback works), NoBig (TCP not available and UDP size limited) and Permissive (passes data known to fail validation).
sections.eli5: Each mail room gets a grade, such as great, okay or please avoid, plus a short note saying what exactly is broken.

sections.title: Working Around the Roadblocks
sections.content:
The RFC ties the labels to avoidance practices but says it does not specify exactly how to do that. It does describe a general fallback sequence:

  1. If a resolver is a Validator or DNSSEC-aware, send queries through it and validate locally. If validation fails, try the next resolver.
  2. If it is Not a DNS Resolver or Non-DNSSEC-capable, mark it unusable and try the next.
  3. If no resolvers remain and direct queries work, iterate from the root. For a SECURE or BOGUS answer, return the result. For an INSECURE one, re-query Non-DNSSEC-capable servers and return their answers without the AD bit set.
  4. Otherwise return an error code and log a failure.

A transport method that worked MUST be remembered, per recursive resolver and per authoritative server, to avoid needless fallbacks. Remembered settings MUST be refreshed periodically and when an error occurs.

For no response, error response or missing DNSSEC metadata, a validator MAY retry with different EDNS0 sizes (4096, 1492 or none), retry with TCP only, iterate from the root, or use an alternative transport known to be supported. For illegal responses (such as referral loops or lame delegations) and bogus responses, it MAY iterate from the root, and for illegal ones also check whether antecedent zones are Insecure. The validator SHOULD remember broken behavior per zone for the zone's SOA-negative TTL, and MAY blacklist misbehaving name servers, timing entries out periodically.

Non-DNSSEC-capable resolvers can still be used in careful ways, for example for known insecure parts of the DNS tree. A resolver that knows NSEC but not NSEC3 is only partially usable and usually lacks unknown-type support, so it is mostly to be avoided.
sections.eli5: If one mail room is bad, try the next one. If all are bad, go to the head post office yourself and do the whole job from the start.

sections.title: Start-Up Problems and the Quick Test
sections.content:
Some situations cause connectivity trouble for validation. After a device has been off, or when it always starts with the same clock time, time synchronization problems appear, for example when it must resolve the name of its own time server. A new connection behind an HTTP paywall (hotels, airports, coffee shops) may have no DNSSEC, validation or even DNS until the user passes forced web pages, and the tests give very different results before and after.

The RFC says there are only two choices. Keep doing DNSSEC processing, which is the most secure but likely makes all DNS requests fail. Or turn DNSSEC off until the network proves usable, which lets the user carry on at the cost of security and opens a denial-of-service route if a man in the middle can convince a device that DNSSEC is impossible. If DNSSEC resolution is not possible, the Host Validator SHOULD log the event or report an error. With no user, it may follow a policy to continue or fail. Continuing silently could make users assume security that does not exist.

A quick test with four queries gives a score: one point per expected answer and a second if the AD bit is set as expected. It tests negative answers for algorithm 5, algorithm 8, algorithm 13, and a name that must fail validation.
sections.eli5: When you arrive somewhere that makes you sign in first, the secure mail does not work yet. You can wait safely, or skip the seals and risk being tricked.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC says only that it discusses problems that may occur while deploying DNSSEC and what may help detect and mitigate them. Following its suggestions is said to give a more secure DNSSEC-operational environment than simply disabling DNSSEC. Section 6 adds the specific warning that falling back to no validation can be exploited by an attacker who convinces a device that DNSSEC is impossible.
sections.eli5: It is safer to find a way around a blocked road than to throw away the lock on your mailbox.

items.label: Passes all DNSSEC tests
items.desc: The AD bit is set appropriately.

items.label: Passes all DNSSEC tests
items.desc: Does not set the AD bit, so it is not validating; fine as a forwarder for a Host Validator.

items.label: Not DNSSEC-aware
items.desc: Hard for a Host Validator to operate behind; may serve known insecure parts of the tree.

items.label: Improperly behaving
items.desc: Should not be used at all.
